Roman armies used the tuba and cornu to give signals in battle and on the march; trumpets also opened games and processions.

Heralds of holy war and warning. Their judgments are partial (a third) and aimed at prompting repentance (9:20-21), in contrast to the final bowls of chapter 16. The seventh trumpet (11:15) announces the kingdom and is often linked with the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16, a link that is itself contested.

Seven sequential judgments in the future seven-year Tribulation, following the seals; dispensationalists (Walvoord, Thomas) generally deny that the seventh trumpet is the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15 because they place the rapture before the Tribulation.

A chronological series across church history: the first four against the western Roman Empire (Goths, Vandals, Huns, the fall of the western emperor in 476), the fifth and sixth against the eastern empire (Saracens and Turks).
The covenant-lawsuit alarm against apostate Jerusalem, sounding through the Jewish War; like Jericho, the "city" falls at the seventh blast.
Recurring warning judgments throughout the age between Christ's comings; the trumpets recapitulate the seals from a different angle and climax at the end.
Another angel with a golden censer at the altar

On the Day of Atonement the high priest took a censer full of coals from the altar and two handfuls of incense into the Holy of Holies (Leviticus 16:12-13); Hebrews 9:4 associates a golden censer with the inner sanctuary. Censers also carried atonement in Numbers 16:46-48, where Aaron stops a plague. Some Jewish traditions describe an angel (often Michael) offering the prayers of the righteous in heaven (Tobit 12:12, 15; 3 Baruch 11-16; Testament of Levi 3:5-6).
Incense burners were standard in Greco-Roman sacrifice and in the imperial cult, where incense offered before the emperor's image was a test of loyalty that Christians refused (Pliny, Letters 10.96).

An angel performs a priestly role in the heavenly temple, presenting the prayers of God's people. The question whether this "other angel" is Christ (as some older Protestant commentators held) is answered no by most modern interpreters, since Revelation never calls Christ an angel and here the angel only assists the saints' prayers.
Several historicists (e.g. Elliott) read the angel as Christ the true High Priest, contrasted with corrupt intercession of saints and clergy in the church of the fourth and fifth centuries.
Usually a created angel ministering in the heavenly temple in the Tribulation period.
Much incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar

The golden altar of incense stood before the veil in the Holy Place (Exodus 30:1-10; 40:5); incense was burned morning and evening with the daily sacrifice, the hour of prayer (Luke 1:9-10; Acts 3:1). Psalm 141:2 asks that prayer rise like incense. Revelation 5:8 has already identified bowls of incense as the saints' prayers, and 6:9-11 placed the martyrs' cry for vindication under the altar.
Incense (frankincense from Arabia) was costly and burned in pagan temples and at imperial ceremonies; in Asia, Christians would have recognised the contrast with offering incense to Caesar.

The trumpet judgments are presented as God's answer to his people's prayers, especially the martyrs' plea "How long?" (6:10). Prayer is not passive: it is part of the means by which God governs history.
The censer filled with altar fire and hurled to the earth

Modelled on Ezekiel 10:2-7, where a man in linen takes coals from between the cherubim and scatters them over Jerusalem as a sign of its coming destruction. Fire from the altar elsewhere signifies divine judgment (Leviticus 10:1-2; Isaiah 6:6-7 for its purifying side).

The same altar that receives prayer becomes the source of judgment: the saints' prayers are answered by fire cast on the earth. The reversal of the censer's direction (up as incense, down as fire) is the theological centre of the chapter.
Because Ezekiel 10 concerns the burning of Jerusalem, preterists such as Chilton see the echo as a signal that the coming judgments target the same city in AD 70.
A pattern of judgment answering the persecuted church's prayers in every era.
Thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake

The Sinai theophany formula (Exodus 19:16-18) with storm, trumpet and quaking mountain. Revelation repeats the formula at 4:5, 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18-21, adding an element each time (earthquake, then hail, then a great earthquake and huge hail), a deliberate crescendo that links the end of each sevenfold series.
Asia Minor was earthquake country: Sardis and Philadelphia were devastated in AD 17, and Laodicea in about AD 60.

A structural marker. Bauckham showed that the escalating storm formula ties the seventh seal, seventh trumpet and seventh bowl to the same climax, which many take as evidence that the three series end at the same point (recapitulation) rather than in simple sequence.
Evidence for recapitulation: each series ends in the final theophany.
Literal cosmic and seismic events, often read with a progressive (telescoping) structure in which each series grows out of the last.
First trumpet: hail and fire mixed with blood

The seventh Egyptian plague (Exodus 9:23-26) of hail with fire flashing through it, which struck plants and trees. Blood and fire together recall Joel 2:30-31 and Ezekiel 38:22 (fire, hail and bloodshed against Gog). Wisdom of Solomon 16:16-22 meditates on fire raging in hail as creation fighting for the righteous.
Burning of crops and orchards was a standard tactic of invading armies in the ancient world.

The first of four judgments on the created order, partial (a third) and patterned on the Exodus: God is again judging an oppressor so as to deliver his people. The note that "all the green grass" burns while 9:4 still mentions grass is often cited to show the visions are not a strictly literal chronicle.
The Gothic invasions under Alaric (c. 400-410), ending in the sack of Rome, a storm from the north on the western empire (Elliott, Barnes).
Devastation of the land of Israel as Roman armies burned crops and trees in the campaign of AD 67-70; Josephus records the stripping of trees around Jerusalem for siege works.
Literal ecological catastrophe in the future Tribulation, possibly by natural or military means.
Recurring natural disasters through history that warn humanity and limit its resources.
A third (of earth, trees, sea, waters, lights, mankind)

Ezekiel 5:2, 12 divides Jerusalem's people into thirds (burned, slain, scattered); Zechariah 13:8-9 has two thirds cut off and a third refined. The fraction thus belongs to prophetic judgment-and-remnant language.

A substantial but limited portion: the trumpets are severe yet not final, greater than the quarter of the fourth seal (6:8) and less than the totality of the bowls. The point is restraint that leaves room for repentance (9:20-21).
Often taken geopolitically as the third of the Roman world (the western empire, then the eastern), following the triple division of the empire.
Usually literal proportions of the earth affected.
A symbolic proportion marking partial, warning judgment.
Second trumpet: something like a great mountain burning, thrown into the sea

Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a destroying mountain that God will make a burnt mountain; Jeremiah 51:42 says the sea will cover her. Jesus speaks of a mountain cast into the sea (Mark 11:23, spoken near the temple mount). 1 Enoch 18:13 and 21:3 describe disobedient stars as "great burning mountains", and Sibylline Oracles 5.158-161 has a great star fall into the sea and burn Babylon (Rome).

Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, destroying Pompeii and darkening the Bay of Naples; Pliny the Younger described the eruption. Sea trade was the lifeblood of Asian cities like Ephesus and Smyrna, so the loss of a third of ships threatened the economy that Revelation 18 later mourns.
A judgment on the sea and its commerce, echoing the first Egyptian plague (water to blood, Exodus 7:20-21). John says "something like" a mountain, signalling a vision rather than a description.

Chilton and others read the mountain as Jerusalem/Mount Zion, the apostate "mountain", cast into the sea of the nations (cf. Mark 11:23); some note the Jewish fleet destroyed at Joppa and the sea of Galilee battle in Josephus (Jewish War 3.9.3; 3.10.9).
Genseric's Vandals, a naval power that ravaged Mediterranean islands and coasts and sacked Rome by sea in 455 (Elliott, Barnes).
Possibly a literal meteor, asteroid or volcanic mass striking the ocean in the Tribulation.
God's judgment on the commercial and maritime structures humans trust, recurring in every age; some see allusion to Babylon's fall (Jeremiah 51).
Third trumpet: a great star named Wormwood

Wormwood (Artemisia, a bitter plant) is a prophetic image of the bitterness of judgment and apostasy: God will make idolatrous Israel drink wormwood and poisoned water (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15); Deuteronomy 29:18 warns of a root bearing poison and wormwood among those who turn to other gods; Amos 5:7 and 6:12 speak of justice turned to wormwood. A fallen star recalls Isaiah 14:12 (the king of Babylon as a fallen morning star) and the fallen watchers of 1 Enoch 86-88. The scene reverses the sweetening of Marah's bitter water (Exodus 15:23-25).

Wormwood was used in antiquity as a medicine and vermifuge and was known to be bitter but not usually lethal, which underlines the symbolic character of the deaths. Popular modern claims that "Chernobyl" means wormwood are inexact (the name refers to mugwort, a related Artemisia) and are not part of scholarly exegesis.

Judgment on fresh water, the source of life, under a name that recalls the punishment of idolatry. The star is probably an agent of judgment (angelic or symbolic) rather than an astronomical body only.
Attila the Hun, "the scourge of God", whose campaigns (c. 440-453) swept the river regions of the Danube, Rhine and Po (Elliott, Barnes).

Apostate Israel itself, or its leadership, fallen from heaven and turning the land's waters bitter, echoing Jeremiah 9:15; Chilton connects it to Deuteronomy 29:18. Josephus describes the Jordan and Galilee choked with corpses in AD 67-68.
A literal celestial body (perhaps a comet or meteor) contaminating water supplies, or a powerful fallen angel.
Recurring judgments by which God lets idolaters taste the bitterness of their idolatry; the false teaching that poisons life.
Fourth trumpet: a third of the sun, moon and stars struck

The ninth Egyptian plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21-23). Prophetic texts use darkened luminaries for the fall of nations and the Day of the Lord (Isaiah 13:10 of Babylon; Ezekiel 32:7-8 of Egypt; Joel 2:10, 31; Amos 8:9). Jesus uses the same idiom in the Olivet Discourse (Matthew 24:29).
Eclipses and astral signs were read in the Roman world as omens of the fall of rulers; Roman writers (Suetonius, Tacitus) record portents around the deaths of emperors.

Darkness is the undoing of the creation of light (Genesis 1:14-18) and a classic sign of political and cosmic upheaval. Interpreters disagree whether the language is primarily literal or the conventional prophetic idiom for the collapse of powers.
The extinction of the western Roman emperorship (Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476) and the eclipse of Rome's consuls and senate, the "lights" of the western third.
De-creation language for the collapse of Israel's political and religious order in AD 70, as in Isaiah 13 for Babylon.
Literal reduction of sunlight and moonlight during the Tribulation.
God's judgment on idolatrous society experienced as darkness and despair, recurring until the end.
An eagle flying in mid-heaven crying "Woe, woe, woe"

Hosea 8:1 sets the trumpet to the mouth because an eagle is over the Lord's house; Deuteronomy 28:49 threatens a nation swooping like an eagle against covenant-breakers; Habakkuk 1:8 likens the Babylonians to eagles. In 2 Baruch 77:17-26 an eagle carries Baruch's letter to the exiles, and in 4 Ezra 11-12 the eagle is Rome. Some later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read "angel" instead of "eagle"; the earliest witnesses read "eagle". "Woe" is the prophetic lament-oracle (Isaiah 5; Amos 5:18).
The eagle (aquila) was the sacred standard of every Roman legion and an emblem of Jupiter; a heavenly eagle announcing doom would strike readers who knew the legions' standards.

A herald (perhaps one of the four living creatures, the third of which is like an eagle, Revelation 4:7) announcing that the last three trumpets are worse and are directed at "those who dwell on the earth", Revelation's phrase for unbelieving humanity hostile to God's people (6:10; 13:8).

Recalls Deuteronomy 28:49 and Hosea 8:1: the covenant curse of an eagle-like (Roman) army falling on Israel; some note the legionary eagles set up in the temple courts in AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.6.1).
The three woes are the Saracen, Turkish and final (often papal or French Revolution era) woe trumpets.
A literal heavenly messenger warning the world in the Tribulation.
Those who dwell on the earth

The phrase echoes Isaiah 24:1-6 and 26:9, 21 (judgment on the earth's inhabitants). In 1 Enoch (e.g. 37:5; 54:9) "those who dwell on the earth" can denote the wicked who are judged, and in Hebrew "the land" (ha-aretz) can mean the land of Israel.
In Revelation the phrase consistently names unbelievers who persecute the saints and worship the beast (6:10; 11:10; 13:8, 12, 14; 17:2, 8). The dispute is over scope.
Translates as "those who dwell on the land", that is, the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem under covenant judgment (Gentry, Chilton).
The unbelieving population of the whole world during the Tribulation.
Humanity whose home and loyalties are in this present order rather than in God.

The trumpets are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 falling on Judea and Jerusalem in the Jewish War (AD 66-70). The fire from the altar recalls Ezekiel 10 and the burning of Jerusalem; the burning mountain cast into the sea is Mount Zion's fall; Wormwood is apostate Israel (Jeremiah 9:15); "those who dwell on the land" are the people of Judea. Chilton and Gentry stress the Jericho pattern: seven trumpets announce the fall of the city that rejected God's messengers. This reading depends on a pre-70 date of Revelation, which is disputed.

The seventh seal opens a new era of judgments on the Roman Empire after its Christianisation. The four trumpets fall on the western third of the empire: Alaric's Goths (first), Genseric's Vandals by sea (second), Attila's Huns along the rivers (third), and the extinction of the western emperor in 476 (fourth), as set out in detail by Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae and Barnes's Notes. The eagle's three woes introduce the Saracens, the Turks and the final judgments.

The trumpets are literal, future judgments in the seven-year Tribulation that follow and intensify the seal judgments, unfolding out of the seventh seal (Walvoord, Thomas). They involve real ecological and astronomical catastrophes on a third of the world; the eagle (or angel) gives a final warning before the demonic woe judgments of chapter 9. Futurists argue that the deliberate echo of the Egyptian plagues, which were real historical events, favours expecting real (if vividly described) catastrophes, and that the escalation from a quarter (6:8) to a third (8:7-12) to the whole (chapter 16) marks a progressive sequence.

The trumpets recapitulate the period between Christ's ascension and return from the angle of warning. Like the Exodus plagues they show God judging an idolatrous world through disasters in nature and society, partially (a third), so that people might repent, while answering the prayers of the persecuted church (Hendriksen, Beale in modified form). The final trumpet, like the final seal and bowl, brings the last judgment.

Many recent commentators (Beale, Osborne, Koester, Keener) combine approaches: the imagery is drawn from the Exodus and prophetic judgment oracles and spoke to first-century Asia (sea trade, Roman power), it describes recurring patterns of judgment through the church age, and it climaxes in the still-future consummation. They typically see the series as overlapping rather than strictly sequential.

Like partial preterists, full preterists place all the trumpets in the period ending in AD 70, but they also identify the seventh trumpet of this series with the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15 and the resurrection, held to have been fulfilled spiritually then. This conclusion places full preterism outside the historic creeds, which confess a future bodily resurrection; proponents reply that Scripture, not the creeds, must govern.
What does it mean that the trumpet judgments are presented as God's answer to the prayers of the saints (Revelation 8:3-5)? How should that shape the way Christians pray about injustice?
Trace the parallels between the first four trumpets and the plagues of Egypt. What does the Exodus pattern suggest about whom the judgments are against and whom they are for?
Why does the text keep limiting the judgments to "a third"? How do the different views explain this restraint?

Does the seventh seal contain the trumpets, or do the seals, trumpets and bowls describe the same period from different angles? What evidence (such as the repeated thunder-earthquake formula) bears on the question?
The fifth and sixth trumpets: locusts from the Abyss and the cavalry from the Euphrates

The fifth trumpet (the first woe) shows a star fallen from heaven that receives the key to the Abyss; smoke pours out, and from it come locust-like creatures with scorpion stings that torment, but may not kill, those without God's seal for five months. Their king is the angel of the Abyss, Abaddon or Apollyon, "Destroyer". The sixth trumpet (the second woe) releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, and a cavalry of two hundred million, with lion-headed horses breathing fire, smoke and sulfur, kills a third of humanity. Yet the survivors do not repent of idolatry, murder, sorcery, sexual immorality or theft, which shows that the trumpets aim at repentance and that judgment alone does not produce it.
Fifth trumpet: the fallen star opens the Abyss
Locusts that torment the unsealed for five months
Description of the locusts and their king Abaddon/Apollyon
The first woe passes
Sixth trumpet: the four angels at the Euphrates released
The two hundred million cavalry
The rest of humanity does not repent

The fifth trumpet expands the eighth Egyptian plague (Exodus 10:12-20) through Joel 1-2, where a locust swarm is described as an invading army with teeth like lions and the appearance of horses, the herald of the Day of the Lord. Locust plagues were a real terror in the ancient Near East and appear among the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:38, 42). The Abyss draws on Second Temple traditions about rebellious angels imprisoned until the judgment (1 Enoch 10:4-6, 18-21, 88; Jubilees 5:6-10; Luke 8:31; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6), so the scene is widely read as a demonic plague released under God's permission and limited by his seal. Abaddon ("destruction") is a poetic name for the realm of the dead in Job, Psalms and Proverbs and is personified in the Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns.

The sixth trumpet turns east. The Euphrates was the ideal border of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18) and the river beyond which Israel's invaders, Assyria and Babylon, came (Isaiah 8:7; Jeremiah 46:10). In the first century it was Rome's frontier with Parthia, whose mounted archers had destroyed Crassus's army at Carrhae (53 BC) and humiliated a Roman force at Rhandeia (AD 62). Parthian horsemen were famed for long hair and for shooting arrows backwards while riding away (the "Parthian shot"), which many see behind the creatures whose power is in their tails. The legend that Nero would return from the east with Parthian armies (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139; 5.361-368; Tacitus, Histories 2.8) and 1 Enoch 56:5-8, where angels stir up the Parthians and Medes against the land, show how charged the Euphrates image was. The vice list in 9:20-21 reflects Jewish polemic against idols that cannot see, hear or walk (Psalm 115:4-7; Daniel 5:23; Wisdom of Solomon 13-15) and the trade-guild idolatry pressed on Christians in Asia.
A star fallen from heaven given the key to the shaft of the Abyss

Stars represent angels in Jewish apocalyptic (Judges 5:20; Job 38:7; Daniel 8:10; Revelation 1:20). 1 Enoch 86-88 portrays the fallen watchers as stars that fall from heaven and are bound in the abyss; Isaiah 14:12 depicts the king of Babylon as a fallen star. Keys signify delegated authority (Isaiah 22:22); in Revelation 1:18 Christ holds the keys of death and Hades and in 20:1 an angel holds the key of the Abyss.

An angelic agent. The perfect tense "had fallen" leads many to see a fallen angel, perhaps Satan (cf. Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:9), though others hold it is simply a good angel descending, as in 20:1. Either way, the key is "given": evil acts only within limits set by God.
Often identified with Muhammad (Barnes, Elliott), or with the apostate influences that opened the way to Islam in the seventh century.
Usually Satan or a fallen angel, literally releasing demonic hordes in the Tribulation (Walvoord).
Satan or a fallen angel, permitted throughout the age to unleash spiritual deception and torment on unbelievers.

Satan or a fallen angel unleashing demonic oppression on apostate Israel during the war years; Chilton links it to Jesus' warning of the unclean spirit returning sevenfold to "this evil generation" (Matthew 12:43-45).
The pit of the Abyss

The Greek abyssos renders the Hebrew tehom, the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2 and Psalm 107:26, and came to mean the underworld prison of evil spirits: 1 Enoch 10:4-6, 13 and 18:11-16 (a chasm of fire where disobedient stars are bound), 21:7-10, Jubilees 5:6-10. Demons beg Jesus not to send them into the Abyss (Luke 8:31). Romans 10:7 uses it for the realm of the dead.
Greek mythology had a parallel in Tartarus, the deep prison of the Titans (2 Peter 2:4 uses the verb "tartarize").
The source of demonic evil and later of the beast (11:7; 17:8) and the place where Satan is bound (20:1-3). Its opening means God permits a measured outbreak of demonic power as judgment.
Smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, darkening sun and air

Smoke from a furnace rose from Sodom and Gomorrah after their destruction (Genesis 19:28) and from Sinai at God's descent (Exodus 19:18). Locust swarms dense enough to darken the land are described in Exodus 10:15 and Joel 2:10.
An image of judgment and spiritual darkness; the darkening may also anticipate the swarm itself, since huge locust clouds literally blot out the sun.
The spread of Islam and its doctrine, which historicists described as darkening the "sun" of the gospel in the East.
Deception and spiritual blindness released on those who reject God.
Locusts with power like scorpions

The eighth Egyptian plague (Exodus 10:4-15) and the locust army of Joel 1-2, a figure for invading nations and the Day of the Lord. Locusts are among the covenant curses for disobedience (Deuteronomy 28:38, 42; 1 Kings 8:37). Scorpions symbolise hostile, painful forces (Ezekiel 2:6; Deuteronomy 8:15; Luke 10:19, where Jesus gives disciples authority over serpents and scorpions). Wisdom of Solomon 16:9 recalls the Egyptians killed by the bites of locusts and flies.

Locust plagues periodically devastated Syria, Palestine and Asia Minor. Scorpions were common in the region, and their sting causes intense pain but is rarely fatal to adults, which fits the limit "torment, not kill". The locust was associated with Apollo, honoured in some places as a locust-averting god (Apollo Parnopios).
A hybrid plague of demonic torment: real locusts eat vegetation, but these are forbidden to touch plants and attack only people, so the image is not of an ordinary insect swarm.

The Saracen (Arab Muslim) armies of the seventh and eighth centuries, coming from Arabia, the land of locust swarms; the order not to hurt grass was compared to Abu Bakr's reported instruction not to destroy palm trees or crops (Barnes, Elliott).
A demonic plague of madness and torment on Judea in the war years, or the Roman siege forces; Chilton stresses demonic oppression and the internal Zealot terror described by Josephus.
Literal demonic beings released in the Tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas); popular writers (e.g. Hal Lindsey) once suggested attack helicopters, a reading most futurist scholars do not adopt.
Demonic forces that torment unbelievers with the inner misery, fear and emptiness of life without God, throughout history (Hendriksen).
Only those without the seal of God on their foreheads harmed

Ezekiel 9:4-6 has a mark (the Hebrew letter tav) put on the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem's abominations, so that they are spared the slaughter. In the Exodus plagues Israel in Goshen was spared (Exodus 8:22; 9:4, 26) and the blood on the doorposts protected the firstborn (Exodus 12:13). Psalms of Solomon 15:6-9 speaks of the mark of God on the righteous for salvation.
Slaves and soldiers in the Roman world could be branded or tattooed to show ownership; seals on documents and goods marked owners' protection.

Refers back to the sealing of the servants of God in 7:3-8. Believers are protected from this spiritual plague (not necessarily from physical suffering or martyrdom, which Revelation expects), while the plague falls on those who bear no mark of belonging to God.
Includes the literal 144,000 Jewish servants sealed in chapter 7, and other believers living in the Tribulation.
All true believers, sealed by the Spirit (Ephesians 1:13), preserved from demonic deception.
The Christian remnant in Judea who heeded Jesus' warning and fled before the siege (Luke 21:20-21; Eusebius, Church History 3.5 on flight to Pella).
Tormented for five months

The lifespan of a locust is about five months, roughly the dry season from spring to late summer. The floodwaters prevailed for 150 days (Genesis 7:24; 8:3). Some see a limited, divinely set period of judgment.
Locust swarms in the eastern Mediterranean typically appear in spring and summer.
A limited, relatively short period of torment, framed by the natural locust season. Interpreters differ on whether it is a literal span or symbolic of a restricted period.

Using the day-for-a-year principle, 150 years of Saracen expansion, often dated from c. 612 (the start of Muhammad's preaching) to 762 (the founding of Baghdad, when the caliphate settled), or similar ranges (Elliott, Barnes).

A literal five-month period in the war, often linked to the five months of Gessius Florus's outrages in AD 66 (May to September) or to the five-month siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 (roughly April to September).
A literal five months within the Tribulation.
A symbolic, limited time: the torment is real but restrained.
People will seek death and not find it

Job 3:21 speaks of those who long for death that does not come; Jeremiah 8:3 says the survivors of judgment will prefer death to life. Hosea 10:8 and Revelation 6:16 have people calling on mountains to cover them.
Suicide was regarded by Stoics as an honourable exit; denying even that escape intensifies the horror.
The torment is psychological and spiritual as much as physical: life becomes unbearable, yet no escape is granted. It portrays the despair of life under judgment without repentance.
Horses prepared for battle, crowns of gold, human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, iron breastplates

Joel 2:4-5 says the locusts look like horses and sound like chariots; Joel 1:6 gives them teeth like a lion's. The resemblance of a locust's head to a horse's head was noticed in antiquity (Italian cavalletta and German Heupferd, "hay-horse", preserve it). The sound of chariots rushing into battle echoes Joel 2:5. Crowns suggest authority to conquer, as with the first rider in Revelation 6:2.
Parthian cavalry were known for long, flowing hair; armoured cavalry (cataphracts) wore scale or iron breastplates. Locusts' antennae could be likened to hair, and their thorax plates to armour.

A nightmarish composite that turns Joel's locust army into an invincible, intelligent, cruel host: human faces suggest intelligence, women's hair perhaps seduction or wildness, lions' teeth ferocity, and iron breastplates invulnerability. The piling up of "like" shows John is describing a visionary image, not a zoological species.
Detailed matches with Arab warriors: turbans like crowns, beards (faces of men), long hair, mounted on horses, armour, as argued by Barnes and Elliott.
A description of grotesque demonic beings, perhaps visible, in the Tribulation.
Either demonic forces or the Roman and Zealot armies, depicted with Joel's locust-army imagery to show the Day of the Lord against Jerusalem.
Symbolic portrait of the power, cunning and cruelty of demonic forces.
Their king, the angel of the Abyss: Abaddon in Hebrew, Apollyon in Greek

Abaddon ("destruction", "place of destruction") is a poetic parallel to Sheol and death (Job 26:6; 28:22; 31:12; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11; 27:20). In the Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns (1QH 11:16-19) the torrents of Belial burst into Abaddon, a step toward personifying it. Proverbs 30:27 observes that locusts have no king, so a king over these locusts marks them as unnatural.

Apollyon ("Destroyer") is probably a pun on Apollo, whose name some ancient writers derived from the verb "to destroy" (apollumi) and whose symbols included the locust. Emperors associated themselves with Apollo, notably Nero (who performed as Apollo the lyre-player) and Augustus; Domitian was also linked to him. Many scholars therefore see a jab at the imperial claim: the god the emperors honour is the destroyer from the pit. The pun is widely accepted but not certain.

The ruler of the demonic locusts, the personification of destruction. Some identify him with Satan, others with a subordinate demon or with the fallen star of 9:1. The bilingual name presents a hellish counterpart to the Lamb who rules.
